question.problem:
A processing tank initially holds $750\,\text{L}$ of water containing $900\,\text{g}$ of dissolved sugar.
A solution containing $18\,\text{g/L}$ of dissolved sugar is pumped into the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ Which differential equation best describes the amount of sugar $Q$ in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins?
question.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the mass of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that a water solution containing $18\,\text{g/L}$ of sugar enters the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(18\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(18\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =108\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $750\,\text{L}$ of water.

- A solution enters the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $6t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed water solution leaves the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $6t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
750+6t-6t=750\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the *concentration* of the water solution at time $t$ is 

$$
\frac{Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(6\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{6Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{125}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =108-\frac{Q}{125}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{125}Q=108.\end{aligned}
$$
